summary: Extends the Session Description Protocol (SDP) with capability negotiation parameters and offer/answer procedures, in a backward compatible way. It allows negotiating alternative transport protocols and attributes, such as Secure RTP or different keying methods. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This framework lets two endpoints offer and choose among alternative ways to carry a media session. It keeps a normal SDP configuration so older endpoints can still proceed.

subtitle: SDP can offer alternative transports and attributes for a media session.

tldr.problem: SDP offer and answer describes one active configuration, so endpoints cannot readily negotiate alternative transports or attributes such as secure media settings.
tldr.mechanism: Six SDP attributes list capabilities and potential configurations; an answer identifies the selected alternative.
tldr.outcome: Older endpoints ignore the new attributes and use the ordinary offer/answer exchange. RFC 6871 later updated this specification.

today: RFC 5939 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2010. It has been updated by RFC 6871.

sections.title: Why SDP Needs Alternatives
sections.content:
Session Description Protocol (SDP) describes media streams and their settings. The offer/answer model lets one side offer a configuration and the other select from it, but the base model does not negotiate alternative transport protocols or attributes.

This limits how endpoints can select combinations such as plain RTP or Secure RTP and their keying attributes. RFC 5939 adds a limited, backward-compatible capability framework; it is not intended as a general-purpose capability system.
sections.plainLanguage: An SDP offer normally describes one setup. This framework lets the offer include other supported setups that the receiver can choose.

sections.title: Capabilities and Configurations
sections.content:
A capability says what an endpoint supports, such as a transport protocol or an SDP attribute. Listing a capability does not mean that the session will use it. A potential configuration combines capabilities into an alternative that can be negotiated.

The actual configuration is the setup already described by the media line and its attributes. The answerer selects the actual configuration or a valid potential configuration, then indicates that choice to the offerer.
sections.plainLanguage: A capability is an available option, while a configuration is a set of options for a session. The answer selects which configuration the endpoints will use.

sections.title: The Six Negotiation Attributes
sections.content:
The framework defines a=csup for supported extensions and a=creq for required extensions. a=acap lists attribute capabilities, and a=tcap lists transport-protocol capabilities.

a=pcfg references capabilities to define potential configurations. A lower configuration number is preferred. The answer uses a=acfg to identify the selected configuration. Unknown attributes are ignored, so endpoints without framework support continue with ordinary SDP processing.
sections.plainLanguage: Four attributes list support and choices. The offer lists possible configurations, and the answer names the one it selected.

sections.title: Referencing Capabilities
sections.content:
Attribute and transport capabilities receive numbers from 1 through 2^31-1, each unique within its own capability namespace across the session description. A potential configuration references these numbers and can include alternatives in preference order.

Potential configurations can add attributes, replace the media-line transport, and delete existing attributes at media level, session level, or both. A capability cannot contain another capability-negotiation attribute, which prevents recursive processing.
sections.plainLanguage: The offer assigns numbers to its options. Each potential configuration uses those numbers to identify the transport and attributes it proposes.

sections.title: Selecting and Applying a Configuration
sections.content:
The answerer checks potential configurations in ascending configuration-number order and chooses the most preferred valid option that local policy permits. The answerer processes the chosen option as an offer, then returns an answer with a=acfg identifying what it used. An answer MUST NOT include a=creq.

If the selected option differs from the original actual configuration, the offerer SHOULD send a follow-up offer making the selected configuration actual. This helps intermediaries that do not understand the capability attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver tries the numbered choices from most preferred to least preferred. It tells the sender which choice worked, so both can use the same setup.

sections.title: Timing, Intermediaries and Security
sections.content:
Media may arrive before the answer tells the offerer which configuration was selected. The RFC recommends sending the answer promptly; preconditions can prevent media from flowing before negotiation finishes. Large sets of alternatives can also consume the answerer's memory and processing time.

An attacker who can alter an offer could force selection of a weaker offered security option. The RFC recommends protecting SDP integrity, ideally end to end. Changing or removing a=acfg can also disrupt negotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: If an attacker can change the offer, the attacker may steer the endpoints toward a weaker option. Protecting the SDP from changes helps prevent this.

messages.label: Follow-up offer using selected setup
messages.note: Recommended when a potential configuration was selected.
